traveler: Jacob Ludwig Carl Grimm and Wilhelm Carl Grimm
title: The Amtshaus to the Letter F: two brothers, one household, and the making of a national memory
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hanau, the house on the Paradeplatz
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wilhelm's birth on 24 February 1786 is folded into this stop rather than given its own
stops.campa: On the fourth of January 1785 a son is born to Philipp Wilhelm Grimm, district official of Hanau, and to Dorothea Grimm born Zimmer, in the house on the market square. They name him Jacob. Thirteen months later, on the twenty-fourth of February 1786, a second son follows and is named Wilhelm. Six of the nine children of this marriage will live past infancy. The house stands on the Paradeplatz, which the town later renames Freiheitsplatz, until a bombing raid on the nineteenth of March 1945 takes it down; a marker on the square now keeps the address.
suggested_refs: The Hanau memorial marker on the Freiheitsplatz, on the site of the destroyed birth house

stops.name: Steinau an der Strasse, the Amtmann's house
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In 1791 the father is appointed Amtmann of Steinau, and the family moves into the official residence, a Renaissance house of 1562 on the road east out of the town. The court sits on the upper floor; the children have the ground. Jacob is six, Wilhelm five. The orchard, the wall, the few streets and the forest beyond them are the whole of the world they can name, and the speech they will spend their lives writing down is the speech of towns this size. The house holds them five years.
suggested_refs: The 1562 Amtshaus at Steinau an der Strasse, now the Brueder Grimm-Haus museum

stops.name: Steinau an der Strasse, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; cause of death given as pneumonia by multiple concurring biographies
stops.campa: On the tenth of January 1796 Philipp Wilhelm Grimm dies of pneumonia at Steinau. The salary stops at once and the residence goes with the office; Dorothea Grimm and six children must leave the Amtshaus. The servants are dismissed and the house is closed. Jacob is eleven and becomes, in fact if not in law, the eldest man of the household. In a single winter the brothers pass from the children of a magistrate to the dependents of relatives, and they stay dependents for the next twelve years.
suggested_refs: Steinau parish death register for Philipp Wilhelm Grimm, January 1796
sources: Standard Grimm biography, concurring on date and cause

stops.name: Kassel, the aunt's house and the Lyceum
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In 1798 the two eldest are sent up to Kassel, to their mother's sister Henriette Zimmer, lady-in-waiting at the Hessian court, so that they can be schooled properly. They enter the Lyceum Fridericianum placed below their years, because Steinau taught them less than Kassel expects, and they close the gap by an application their masters remark on. They are charity pupils in a court city, seated apart from the sons of the nobility. Jacob is thirteen, Wilhelm twelve, and they will not be separated again for sixty-one years.
suggested_refs: Enrolment records of the Lyceum Fridericianum, Kassel, 1798

segments.name: Marburg, and the turn from law

stops.name: Marburg, the law faculty
stops.date_confidence: year attested for Jacob; Wilhelm follows in 1803; months not attested
stops.campa: Jacob matriculates at Marburg in 1802 to read law, his father's profession and the family's only route back to standing. Wilhelm follows in 1803. The stipends of the university go to students of noble birth; the sons of a dead district official are told they do not qualify, and Jacob records the refusal with a bitterness that does not fade. They read law dutifully. The university is small and its faculty old. One of its professors is Friedrich Carl von Savigny.
suggested_refs: Matriculation registers of the Alte Universitaet Marburg, 1802 and 1803

stops.name: Marburg, Savigny opens his library
stops.date_confidence: the influence runs 1803-1805; the single date is a convention, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Friedrich Carl von Savigny, young and already teaching the history of Roman law as a living growth rather than a code, gives Jacob the run of his private library. In it Jacob finds Bodmer's edition of the Minnesingers, medieval German verse in print, and reads it as evidence that the language has a written past which nobody has gone through. Savigny teaches that law grows out of a people instead of being imposed on it. The brothers take the method whole and apply it to language.
suggested_refs: The Savigny-Grimm correspondence, cited throughout Grimm scholarship but not consulted directly for this file
sources: Standard Grimm biography on the Savigny influence

stops.name: Paris, the Bibliotheque imperiale on the rue de Richelieu
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Savigny, at work on his history of Roman law in the Middle Ages, sends for Jacob to help him read manuscripts in Paris. It is the first time either brother leaves the German lands. Jacob spends the season in the manuscript room on the rue de Richelieu, copying and collating, learning what an archive is and how a scholar takes a text apart. He is twenty. He goes home to Kassel a philologist who has not yet said so. He will be sent back to these rooms in 1815, to take manuscripts out of them.
suggested_refs: Savigny's Geschichte des roemischen Rechts im Mittelalter, whose Paris research Jacob assisted

stops.name: Kassel, the household regathered
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month inferred from the return from Paris, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Dorothea Grimm brings the younger children to Kassel, and Jacob, back from Paris, joins them; for the first time since Steinau the family lives under one roof. Jacob takes clerical work at the Hessian war office to keep them fed. Wilhelm, whose health has begun the long failing that will shadow him, studies at home. The apartment is small and the money is short, and in it the two brothers begin, without announcing a project, to write down the stories that the women of Kassel tell them.
stops.quote: Concerning our methods of collecting material, it was faithfulness and truthfulness which mattered most to us.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the second edition of the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen (1819), trans. Jonathan Skolnik, German History in Documents and Images
suggested_refs: The Grimm family apartment in Kassel, 1805, first shared household since Steinau

stops.name: Kassel, the Wild pharmacy on the Marktgasse
stops.date_confidence: the association runs from about 1805 to the marriage of 1825; the single date is a convention
stops.campa: Brentano and Achim von Arnim have printed Des Knaben Wunderhorn, a sheaf of old songs gathered as one gathers plants, and the brothers take the lesson. They begin writing tales down. The nearest source is the pharmacist's household on the Marktgasse: the Wild daughters tell what their nurse and their mother told them. Dortchen Wild gives them Frau Holle, Hansel and Gretel, the singing bone. She is a girl of the neighbourhood in a town they can cross on foot. Wilhelm will marry her in twenty years.
stops.quote: After a storm or another misfortune from the heavens has knocked an entire field of growing crops to the ground, it is possible that near some low hedges or bushes a small safe place can be found where a few growing spikes remain.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the second edition of the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen (1819), trans. Jonathan Skolnik, German History in Documents and Images
suggested_refs: Heinz Roelleke's source studies identifying the Wild family contributions to the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen
sources: Roelleke and other source-critical Grimm scholarship on the informants

stops.name: Kassel, the Hassenpflug parlour
stops.date_confidence: the association runs from about 1806 to 1813; the single date is a convention
stops.campa: Down the street the Hassenpflugs, a Kassel family of Huguenot descent, supply Marie and Jeanette and Amalie, who tell the brothers Little Red Riding Hood, Sleeping Beauty, Puss in Boots. The daughters are educated, French is spoken in the house, and Perrault has been read in it. Later scholarship will hold these tales up as proof that the collection is not a transcript of German peasant memory but a room of literate young women repeating what books and nurses gave them. The brothers print them as folk tales.
stops.quote: We have sought to keep every unique feature that we noticed, so that in this way, too, the collection could be given over to nature's diversity.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the second edition of the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen (1819), trans. Jonathan Skolnik, German History in Documents and Images
suggested_refs: Roelleke's identification of the Huguenot informants and the French literary layer in the collection
sources: Heinz Roelleke and other source-critical Grimm scholarship

stops.name: Kassel, librarian to Jerome Bonaparte at Napoleonshoehe
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the pool wrongly sited this at the Palais Bellevue, corrected here to Schloss Napoleonshoehe
stops.campa: Napoleon has made his brother Jerome king of a new Westphalia and seated him at Kassel, in the palace of the Hessian electors, renamed Napoleonshoehe. In 1808 Jacob is appointed superintendent of the royal private library at a salary that keeps the family. He serves a French king in a German capital, spending the paid hours among books and the unpaid hours taking down German tales. The following year the king adds a place as auditor to the state council. The tales taken down on that salary are printed four years later.
suggested_refs: Schloss Wilhelmshoehe, renamed Napoleonshoehe under the Kingdom of Westphalia, seat of Jerome Bonaparte's library

stops.name: Kassel, the mother dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of May 1808 Dorothea Grimm dies. Jacob is twenty-three and now stands as head of the house in law as well as in habit: four younger brothers and a sister to place, feed, and school, on a librarian's salary from a king he does not want. Ludwig Emil, the youngest but one, is sent to study drawing and will spend his life making the portraits by which the family is now known by sight. The brothers work at the tales in the evenings, the only hours nobody else has a claim on.
suggested_refs: Ludwig Emil Grimm's drawings and etchings of the family, the visual record of the household
sources: WebSearch summary of Grimm biographies (worldoftales.com / uc.edu)

stops.name: Niederzwehren, the tailor's widow
stops.date_confidence: the sessions run about 1813-1815; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Dorothea Viehmann, a tailor's widow of Huguenot stock living in the village of Niederzwehren, comes into Kassel to sell garden produce and stays to talk. She tells the brothers tale after tale, and tells them the same way twice, which is what they have been waiting for: a teller whose memory holds its shape. Wilhelm names her in the preface of 1819 and prints Ludwig Emil's portrait of her at the front of the book. She becomes, for a century, the face of the German peasant storyteller.
stops.quote: It was one of those lucky coincidences that we happened to make the acquaintance of a peasant woman in Niederzwehrn, a village near Kassel, who recounted the best and greater part of the fairy tales in the second volume.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the second edition of the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen (1819), trans. Jonathan Skolnik, German History in Documents and Images
suggested_refs: Ludwig Emil Grimm's portrait of Dorothea Viehmann, frontispiece to the second volume from 1819
sources: Wilhelm Grimm's preface to the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen, 2nd ed. (1819)

stops.name: Boekendorf, the Haxthausen circle
stops.date_confidence: the circle runs 1810-1834; month and day defaulted; coordinate corrected from the research pool, which was 11 km off
stops.campa: At Schloss Boekerhof in Westphalia the Haxthausen family keeps an open house for a circle of collectors and poets: the Haxthausen brothers, Annette and Jenny von Droste-Huelshoff, Brentano, and both Grimms. The talk runs from 1810 to 1834, and the Westphalian tales that reach the collection come through this room. They are drier than the Hessian ones, harder in outline, and they widen the book past the districts the brothers can walk to. The gathering is a house party, not a field expedition.
stops.quote: Gleaned one by one, carefully bound together, and valued more than whole sheaves, they are carried home. They provide sustenance for the winter and are perhaps the only seeds for the future.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the second edition of the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen (1819), trans. Jonathan Skolnik, German History in Documents and Images
suggested_refs: Schloss Boekerhof and the Boekendorfer Romantikerkreis, 1810-1834
sources: Roelleke and other Grimm source-critical scholarship on the Haxthausen contributions

stops.name: Berlin, the Realschulbuchhandlung prints volume one
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twentieth of December 1812 the Realschulbuchhandlung of Berlin issues Kinder- und Hausmaerchen, eighty-six numbered tales, dedicated to Bettina von Arnim. It is a scholar's book: notes, variants, no illustrations, and a preface arguing that these fragments are the last unbroken thread of a German past. It is not written for children and it does not sell like a children's book. Within a generation it will be the most printed book in the German language after Luther's Bible, and the brothers will revise it for forty years.
stops.quote: Our first aim in collecting these stories has been exactness and truth. We have added nothing of our own, have embellished no incident or feature of the story, but have given its substance just as we ourselves received it.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen, 2nd ed. (1819), trans. Margaret Hunt, Grimm's Household Tales, vol. 1 (1884)
suggested_refs: The 1812 first edition of Kinder- und Hausmaerchen, inscribed by UNESCO in 2005 on the Memory of the World Register
sources: Publication record of Kinder- und Hausmaerchen vol. 1 (1812)

stops.name: Vienna, the Hofburg and the Congress
stops.date_confidence: the Congress runs September 1814 to June 1815; the research pool wrongly compressed Vienna and the Paris mission into one 1814 entry
stops.campa: Napoleon is beaten and Europe is redrawn at the Hofburg. Jacob attends as secretary of the legation of Electoral Hesse, from September 1814 to June 1815, watching sovereigns trade provinces across a table. He does his diplomatic duty, keeps up his philological correspondence at night, and takes from the Congress a conviction he holds for the rest of his life: that the German lands are one nation whatever the map says, and that the proof lies in the language rather than in any treaty signed in this building.
suggested_refs: Legation records of Electoral Hesse at the Congress of Vienna, 1814-1815
sources: Congress of Vienna legation records for Electoral Hesse

stops.name: Paris, the looted manuscripts
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01; coordinate inherited from the corpus's canonical Paris pin
stops.campa: The peace requires France to give back what its armies carried off. Jacob is sent to Paris a second time, ten years after Savigny brought him, now as the official of a victorious state, to identify and reclaim manuscripts and books taken from German libraries. He walks the same rooms as a claimant instead of a student. He recovers Hessian and other German holdings and goes home with the settled view that a nation's manuscripts are its property in the same sense as its territory.
suggested_refs: French restitution records of 1815 following the Second Treaty of Paris
sources: Corpus canonical Paris pin: gauss.journey.json, max_muller.journey.json, christian_rosenkreuz.journey.json

stops.name: Berlin, volume two
stops.date_confidence: 1815 attested by the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin and de.wikisource; the research pool's claim of an 1814 issue with an 1815 title page is unsupported and was discarded
stops.campa: The second volume appears in Berlin in 1815, seventy further tales, most of them from the Kassel circle and from Dorothea Viehmann. With it the brothers settle into the practice that will define the work: not a fixed text but a text under permanent revision. Wilhelm smooths the prose, joins variants into single tales, and tunes the sentences until they can be said aloud. Jacob turns toward grammar and leaves the tales increasingly to his brother. Five further editions will follow this one in their lifetimes.
stops.quote: Where they complemented each other and no contradictions were there to be eliminated, we combined several tales into one.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the second edition of the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen (1819), trans. Jonathan Skolnik, German History in Documents and Images
suggested_refs: Kinder- und Hausmaerchen vol. 2, Realschulbuchhandlung, Berlin 1815
sources: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, 'Die Erstausgabe der Kinder- und Hausmaerchen'

stops.name: Kassel, the Electoral Library
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In 1816 both brothers take posts at the Electoral Library of Kassel, Jacob as second librarian under Voelkel, Wilhelm as secretary. The pay is small and the work is exactly what they want: thirteen years of shelves, in a court city where Johann Tischbein learned to paint one generation before them. The library's successor, the Murhardsche Bibliothek, will stand on a square named Brueder-Grimm-Platz and hold two manuscript copies of the Splendor Solis, so that Salomon Trismosin and the Grimms share one address across three centuries.
suggested_refs: The Murhardsche Bibliothek on Brueder-Grimm-Platz, Kassel, successor of the Electoral Library

stops.name: Kassel, the first part of the Deutsche Grammatik
stops.date_confidence: year attested; further volumes follow to 1837; the priority dispute with Rasmus Rask is untouched by every source in the research pool
stops.campa: Jacob publishes the first part of the Deutsche Grammatik in 1819 and keeps building it until 1837. In it he sets out, with tables of correspondence across Gothic, Old High German, and the rest, the regular consonant shift that separates the Germanic tongues from their relatives; the shift takes his name. Sound change, he shows, is not decay but law, and law can be read backwards into a past that has left no documents. Comparative philology begins here, and Max Mueller will hold its first Oxford chair.
stops.quote: One may fairly say, that to deny the reality of this mythology is as much as to impugn the high antiquity and the continuity of our language.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Grimm, preface to Deutsche Mythologie, 2nd ed. (1844), trans. James Steven Stallybrass, Teutonic Mythology (1880-88); written of the mythology, quoted here for the argument the Grammatik establishes
suggested_refs: Deutsche Grammatik, part one (1819), and the consonant-shift tables now called Grimm's Law

stops.name: Kassel, the Martinskirche: Wilhelm marries Dortchen
stops.date_confidence: date widely documented; the Martinskirche as venue is tradition rather than a cited record
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of May 1825 Wilhelm marries Henriette Dorothea Wild, called Dortchen, of the pharmacist's household on the Marktgasse, whose tales he printed thirteen years before. He is thirty-nine. Jacob, who never marries, does not move out; he takes rooms in the same apartment and stays there for the remaining thirty-eight years of his life, at the next desk. Four children will be born to Wilhelm and Dortchen. The household that produces the German dictionary is one kitchen and two studies.
suggested_refs: The Martinskirche at Kassel, traditional site of the 1825 marriage

stops.name: Kassel, the post withheld
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Voelkel dies in 1828 and the head librarianship of Kassel, which Jacob has served under for twelve years and expects as a matter of course, goes to another man. It is a small municipal slight and it moves both brothers out of Hesse for good. Jacob is forty-three, author of the Grammatik, known across Europe, and passed over in his own town. When Goettingen writes the following year, he does not need persuading. He resigns his post, and the whole household follows him north.
suggested_refs: The Kassel librarianship of 1828, the appointment that sent the Grimms to Hanover

stops.name: Goettingen, Die deutsche Heldensage
stops.date_confidence: year attested; place corrected to Goettingen alone, the research pool's 'Goettingen/Leipzig' being wrong
stops.campa: Wilhelm's chief work under his own name alone is printed at Goettingen in 1829 by the Dieterichsche Buchhandlung: Die deutsche Heldensage, a gathering of every reference to the Germanic heroic legends he can find in the sources from the sixth century to the sixteenth, arranged so that a lost body of poetry can be seen through its citations. He is doing for the heroes what the two of them did for the tales, salvaging a whole out of surviving pieces. The book arrives at Goettingen before its author does.
stops.quote: Much then is irrecoverably lost to our mythology; I turn to the sources that remain to it, which are partly Written Memorials, partly the never resting stream of living Manners and Story.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Grimm, preface to Deutsche Mythologie, 2nd ed. (1844), trans. James Steven Stallybrass, Teutonic Mythology (1880-88); Jacob's statement of the salvage method his brother applies here to the heroic legends
suggested_refs: Die deutsche Heldensage, Goettingen, Dieterichsche Buchhandlung, 1829; second and expanded edition Berlin, Duemmler, 1867
sources: Title-page copies in ETH-Bibliothek e-rara, Internet Archive, and ZVAB antiquarian records

stops.name: Goettingen, the two appointments
stops.date_confidence: contested: the research pool gives 1829 in one lens and 1830-1837 in another, Britannica gives 1830, de.wikipedia gives Wilhelm's start as 1831; 1830 pinned and the disagreement carried unresolved
stops.campa: The brothers leave Hesse. Jacob is made professor and head librarian of the Georgia Augusta, the post Kassel denied him; Wilhelm comes as under-librarian and is made professor in his turn. Jacob lectures on German grammar, on legal antiquities, on the history of the language, to rooms of students who have never heard these treated as subjects at all. The household moves entire, Dortchen and the children included. They have seven years in Hanover, and the Deutsche Mythologie and the later volumes of the Grammatik come out of them.
suggested_refs: University of Goettingen appointment records for Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, 1830-1831

stops.name: Goettingen, the Deutsche Mythologie
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01; the attached quote is from the preface to the second edition of 1844, not the first
stops.campa: In 1835 Jacob publishes Deutsche Mythologie, an attempt to reassemble the pre-Christian belief of the Germanic peoples out of whatever survived it: place names, charms, court records of witchcraft, proverbs, the vocabulary of the seasons, the shape of a superstition still current in a Hessian village. There is no scripture and no temple to work from. He argues that the language itself is the document, and that gods can be dug out of grammar. The book founds the study of Germanic religion.
stops.quote: Divinities form the core of all mythology: ours were buried almost out of sight, and had to be dug out.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Grimm, preface to Deutsche Mythologie, 2nd ed. (1844), trans. James Steven Stallybrass, Teutonic Mythology (1880-88)
suggested_refs: Deutsche Mythologie (1835), and Stallybrass's English Teutonic Mythology (1880-88)
sources: archive.org full-text scan of Stallybrass's translation

stops.name: Goettingen, the protest of the Seven
stops.date_confidence: month attested as November 1837; day defaulted to 01; coordinate inherited byte-identical from gauss.journey.json
stops.campa: Ernst August, newly king of Hanover, sets aside the constitution of 1833 and requires the university's officers to swear to him personally. In November 1837 seven professors sign a formal declaration that their oath to the constitution binds them and cannot be dissolved by the man who broke it. Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm are two of the seven. The others are Dahlmann, Gervinus, Albrecht, Ewald, and the physicist Wilhelm Weber, whose telegraph wire runs across the roofs to the observatory of Carl Friedrich Gauss.
suggested_refs: The declaration of the Goettinger Sieben, November 1837
sources: Corpus interlock: gauss.journey.json, which narrates the same dismissal through Wilhelm Weber and does not name the Grimms

stops.name: Goettingen, dismissal and banishment
stops.date_confidence: month attested; day defaulted to 01; coordinate inherited byte-identical from gauss.journey.json
stops.campa: All seven are stripped of their chairs. Three of them, Jacob among them, are given days to leave the kingdom of Hanover altogether. He crosses the frontier in December 1837 with Dahlmann and Gervinus, seen off by students; Wilhelm follows with the household. The German states read the affair as the first public stand of professors against a prince, and subscription funds are raised for the seven across the country. Jacob is fifty-two, unemployed, and better known for this than for the Grammatik.
suggested_refs: The subscription funds raised across the German states for the dismissed Goettingen Seven, 1838

stops.name: Kassel, the return without posts
stops.date_confidence: the exile runs 1837-1841; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: They go back to Kassel, the city that passed Jacob over, and live there three years on savings, on the fees of a few publications, and on money raised by admirers who consider them the conscience of the German professoriate. Wilhelm's health is poor and the children are young. No German government will employ two men banished by a king. It is the only long stretch of their adult lives in which neither of them holds an office, and it is when the largest of all their projects is begun.
suggested_refs: The Kassel years of 1837-1841, the Grimms' only period without office

stops.name: Kassel, the dictionary is begun
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month inferred, day defaulted; the research pool's geography lens wrongly placed this at Frankfurt am Main, contradicting its own chronology, and the Frankfurt pin was dropped
stops.campa: The publishers Weidmann propose a dictionary of the German language. The brothers accept, imagining a labour of some ten years: every word from Luther to Goethe, each with its history, its cognates, and its quotations set out in order, so that a nation which has no single state can at least be shown to have one language. Martin Luther's Bible is the floor the whole structure stands on and its most cited authority. Jacob takes A, B, C and F; Wilhelm takes D and E. They are fifty-three and fifty-two.
suggested_refs: The Weidmann contract for the Deutsches Woerterbuch, 1838, and Jacob's preface to volume one (1854)

stops.name: Berlin, the King of Prussia sends for them
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the invitation; residence and academy posts taken up from 1841
stops.campa: Friedrich Wilhelm IV comes to the Prussian throne in 1840, and one of his first acts is to call the Grimms to Berlin. They are elected to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, given salaries and the right to lecture at the university without the duty of holding chairs, and told to go on with their work. Three years after being run out of Hanover for defending a constitution, they are pensioners of a king. They take the offer, move the household to Berlin in 1841, and never leave the city again.
suggested_refs: Prussian Academy of Sciences membership records for Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, 1841

stops.name: Berlin, Unter den Linden: Andersen calls and is not known
stops.date_confidence: date taken from hans_christian_andersen.journey.json, which itself flags that secondary sources place the meeting in 1845-46; coordinate inherited byte-identical from that file
stops.campa: Hans Christian Andersen, in Berlin and certain that the greatest living collector of fairy tales will want to meet him, presents himself without a letter of introduction. Jacob Grimm receives him and has never heard his name. Andersen leaves the house scalded and writes the humiliation down. The two traditions of the European fairy tale, the collected and the invented, stand in one doorway for a quarter of an hour and fail to recognize each other. They will be bound together afterwards in every list anybody makes.
suggested_refs: Andersen's own account of the Berlin call, in his diaries and autobiography
sources: Corpus interlock: hans_christian_andersen.journey.json, stop 'Berlin, Unter den Linden: Grimm has not heard of him'

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Paulskirche
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not in the research pool, defaulted
stops.campa: Revolution reaches the German states, and an elected parliament gathers in the Paulskirche at Frankfurt to make one country out of thirty-nine. Jacob Grimm sits in it as a member, given a place in the front row by acclamation, and speaks for a constitution with a bill of rights, for a Germany defined by the language its people speak rather than by dynastic borders. The assembly offers a crown that is refused, and dissolves without a state. He goes back to Berlin and to the letter A.
suggested_refs: Membership records of the Frankfurt National Assembly, 1848-1849

stops.name: Leipzig, the first volume comes off the press
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted; no Leipzig coordinate exists in the research pool, so a standard city centroid is used and declared in the report
stops.campa: Sixteen years after they took the commission, the first volume of the Deutsches Woerterbuch is printed at Leipzig. Jacob's preface explains what the thing is for, in a tone closer to a national address than to lexicography, and admits how far the scale has run past the estimate. Every word is given with its whole documented history, and every meaning is tracked through quotation from the sources. At this rate the alphabet will take a century to finish. It will take rather more than that.
suggested_refs: Deutsches Woerterbuch, vol. 1, Leipzig 1854, with Jacob Grimm's preface

stops.name: Berlin, the seventh edition
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the research pool gave the place as 'Goettingen/Berlin', which is not a place, and Berlin is pinned because the brothers were living there
stops.campa: The last edition of Kinder- und Hausmaerchen to appear in the brothers' lifetime is published in 1857: two hundred numbered tales and ten children's legends, the text worked over by Wilhelm for forty-five years. Between the first printing and this one the cruelty has been redistributed, mothers have become stepmothers, the pious have grown more pious, and the sentences have been tuned until they can be read aloud to a child without stumbling. The book that began as evidence has become literature.
suggested_refs: The seventh and final lifetime edition of the Kinder- und Hausmaerchen, 1857

stops.name: Berlin, Wilhelm dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Wilhelm Grimm dies in Berlin on the sixteenth of December 1859, of an infection, aged seventy-three. He has carried the tales through seven editions and the dictionary as far as the letter D. Jacob, who has shared a roof with him since 1798 and a desk since 1825, delivers the memorial address to the Academy himself and can barely get through it. He goes on with the work in the same rooms, at the same hours, in a household that keeps his brother's chair where his brother left it.
suggested_refs: Jacob Grimm's memorial address on his brother, delivered to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, 1860

stops.name: Berlin, Jacob dies at the desk
stops.date_confidence: attested; the account that his last entry was the word Frucht is tradition, marked as reported in the sources themselves
stops.campa: Jacob Grimm dies in Berlin on the twentieth of September 1863, aged seventy-eight, four years after his brother and still at work on the dictionary. The story told afterwards is that the last word under his hand was Frucht, fruit. The Grammatik, the Mythologie and the law of sound change are behind him. The dictionary he took on in 1838 as a ten-year job has taken twenty-five years and stands at the letter F, and he leaves it there for other men to carry.
stops.quote: I wish to explain all I can, but I am far from being able to explain all I wish.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Grimm, preface to Deutsche Mythologie, 2nd ed. (1844), trans. James Steven Stallybrass, Teutonic Mythology (1880-88)
suggested_refs: The unfinished manuscript of the Deutsches Woerterbuch at the letter F, September 1863

stops.name: London, Edgar Taylor and the Cruikshank plates
stops.date_confidence: publication runs 1823-1826; month and day defaulted; the stop sits in the afterlife segment because it belongs to the reception rather than to the life, and the segment runs in date order from it
stops.campa: Edgar Taylor prints German Popular Stories at London in 1823, the first English translation, with etchings by George Cruikshank. He Anglicizes the names, cuts the religion, softens the blood and drops the scholarly apparatus. What is left is the illustrated fairy-tale book, the first of its kind. The Grimms, shown the plates, are delighted and commission illustrations of their own. The English-speaking world meets the tales in this edited and decorated form before any other.
suggested_refs: German Popular Stories, trans. Edgar Taylor, illus. George Cruikshank, London 1823-1826
sources: Project MUSE review of the Zipes edition

stops.name: Berlin-Schoeneberg, the graves at the Alter St.-Matthaeus-Kirchhof
stops.date_confidence: burial date not attested in the research pool; defaulted to days after Jacob's death; coordinate taken from de.wikipedia after two conflicting values in the pool
stops.campa: The brothers lie side by side in the churchyard of St. Matthew in Schoeneberg, under plain dark columns of matching design, Wilhelm from 1859 and Jacob from 1863. The city later marks both as graves of honour. Around them stand the elaborate monuments of nineteenth-century Berliners who were richer and are forgotten. Herman Grimm, Wilhelm's son, the art historian who writes the life of Michelangelo, is buried in the same ground, though the claim of four Grimm columns in a row is not borne out by the cemetery lists.
suggested_refs: The Grimm Ehrengraeber at the Alter St.-Matthaeus-Kirchhof, Grossgoerschenstrasse, Berlin-Schoeneberg

stops.name: Hanau, the monument on the Neustaedter Marktplatz
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In 1896 Hanau unveils Syrius Eberle's bronze in front of the town hall: the two brothers, Wilhelm seated with a book open on his knee and Jacob standing beside him with a hand on the back of the chair, the arrangement of a lifetime cast in metal. The town they left at six and five claims them back. The birth house on the other square will be gone in forty-nine years; the statue outlives the raid that takes it and stands over the rebuilding. Every fairy-tale route in Germany now starts at this pedestal.
suggested_refs: The Brothers Grimm National Monument by Syrius Eberle, Neustaedter Marktplatz, Hanau, 1896

stops.name: Berlin, the tales conscripted
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout: the Nazi readings rest on secondary discussion, and no primary occupation-government order for the 1946 ban was reachable
stops.campa: Under the Reich the tales are read as racial instruction: Rotkaeppchen as German innocence stalked by an alien predator, the collection as evidence of a Volk with a character of its own, the tale of the Jew among the thorns useful exactly as it stands. After the war the British occupation authorities are said to have forbidden their publication in the British zone in 1946, judging that these stories helped condition a people to savagery. The order, if it existed, did not hold. The books came back.
suggested_refs: Wartime German press readings of the tales, and the reported 1946 publication ban in the British zone
sources: Tales of Faerie blog citing wartime press coverage; academia.edu discussion
TES Magazine, 'Banned Grimm tales survive the censors'

stops.name: Leipzig, the dictionary finished
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01; the Leipzig coordinate is a standard city centroid supplied from outside the research pool
stops.campa: The Deutsches Woerterbuch is completed in 1961, one hundred and twenty-three years after two unemployed brothers in Kassel agreed to a ten-year job: thirty-three volumes, some three hundred and twenty thousand entries, four generations of scholars, two world wars, and a divided country working on it from both sides. UNESCO inscribes the tales beside Luther's Bible as the best known work of German cultural history. L. Frank Baum, introducing the book that gave America its own fairyland, names the winged fairies of Grimm and Andersen as the thing he means to succeed.
suggested_refs: The completed Deutsches Woerterbuch, 33 volumes, 1838-1961; the UNESCO Memory of the World inscription of 2005
sources: UNESCO Memory of the World register

stops.name: Sababurg, the castle in the Reinhardswald
stops.date_confidence: the association is undated tradition; pinned here to the conventional founding year of the Deutsche Maerchenstrasse, itself unconfirmed; coordinate corrected from the research pool, which was 11 km off
stops.campa: A ruined hunting lodge stands in the Reinhardswald north of Kassel, overgrown, with a wall of thorn around it. Nobody in the brothers' generation connects it to Dornroeschen. The connection is made later, by a region that discovers it owns the birthplace of the world's fairy tales and builds a road six hundred kilometres long from Hanau to Bremen to say so. The castle now takes bookings. No informant, no letter, and no manuscript ties the sleeping princess to this hill.

sources: Deutsche Maerchenstrasse tourist tradition; no primary Grimm-era source ties any tale to these castles

stops.name: Steinau an der Strasse, the Amtshaus becomes a museum
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Renaissance house where the family lived from 1791 to 1796 opens in 1998 as the Brueder Grimm-Haus. The court room upstairs holds exhibits; the ground floor where the children slept holds the tales. One room is given to Ludwig Emil Grimm, the brother who drew, whose portraits of Dorothea Viehmann and of Jacob and Wilhelm at their work are the reason anyone knows what these people looked like. It is the second stop on the Maerchenstrasse and the first house that was ever theirs.
suggested_refs: Brueder Grimm-Haus, Brueder-Grimm-Strasse 80, Steinau an der Strasse, opened 1998

stops.name: Kassel, Grimmwelt on the Weinberg
stops.date_confidence: opening in September 2015; day defaulted; coordinate corrected, the research pool giving three different values none of which match Weinbergstrasse 21
stops.campa: Kassel opens Grimmwelt in September 2015 on the Weinberg hill, a building set into the slope, arranged not by chronology but around twenty-five headwords taken from the Deutsches Woerterbuch. The city's own Grimm manuscripts are shown there. It replaces the older museum in the Palais Bellevue and settles a long argument about which of the two Grimms Kassel is commemorating, by commemorating the dictionary instead of the tales. The library years, not the collecting years, are what this city can claim outright.
